title: Normalized root homomorphisms in semisimple rank at most two
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $P_i=(G_i,T_i=D_A(M_i),\Phi_i,\Phi_i^\vee,\Delta_i,(X_{i,\alpha}))$, $i=0,1$, pinned split realizations [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization], with $|\Delta_i|\leq2$. Suppose $h:M_0\hookrightarrow M_1$ has finite cokernel and $b:\Phi_1\to\Phi_0$ is a bijection carrying $\Delta_1$ onto $\Delta_0$, with $h(b(\alpha))=\alpha$ and $h^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=b(\alpha)^\vee$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi_1$. There is a unique homomorphism $g:G_1\to G_0$ restricting to the constant monomial map $D_A(h)$ [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group] on $T_1$ and satisfying $dg(X_{1,\alpha})=X_{0,b(\alpha)}$ for every $\alpha\in\Delta_1$.

This construction respects passage to full-torus centralizers of simple-root subsystems: for $J\subseteq\Delta_1$, put $L_{1,J}=M_1\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}(J)$, $L_{0,b(J)}=M_0\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}(b(J))$, and $G_{i,J}=Z_{G_i}(D_A(M_i/L_{i,J}))$ (using $b(J)$ for the index on side $0$). These are pinned split realizations with their original torus, roots in the indicated rational span, and the inherited pinning. Then $g(G_{1,J})\subseteq G_{0,b(J)}$ scheme-theoretically and $g|_{G_{1,J}}$ is the same normalized homomorphism for these restricted data. No invertibility of any integer in $A$ is required; empty roots and nontrivial central tori are allowed.

source.place: Example 6.2.6, printed pp.203--204 (rank one); Lemma 6.2.8 and Step 4 of the proof of the Isogeny Theorem, pp.207--209, restricted to root exponents one; normalization and restriction in Step 1, p.205. Only the rank-zero, rank-one and rank-two statement is used here. Read online; local PDF WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group theorem.

proof.text:
Put $f_T=D_A(h)$. Since $h$ is injective and has finite cokernel, $h_{\mathbf Q}$ is an isomorphism. The equality $h(b(\gamma))=\gamma$ therefore identifies signed integral root expansions and positive-root labels. Also
$$\langle h(m),\alpha^\vee\rangle=\langle m,b(\alpha)^\vee\rangle,\qquad h(s_{b(\alpha)}m)=s_\alpha h(m).$$
Thus $b$ preserves the Cartan integers, simple reflections and their orders; enumerate the two bases correspondingly. The monomial definition gives $b(\alpha)(f_T(t))=\alpha(t)$ and $f_T\circ\alpha^\vee=b(\alpha)^\vee$. These are identities on every algebra, including when the characteristic divides the index of $h$.

source.place: Example 6.2.6, pp.203--204, root exponent one; equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.3), p.201

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-low-rank-universal-root-coordinates] on both groups with these corresponding enumerations. Write $x_{i,\gamma}$ for the resulting positive-root maps and $n_{i,\alpha}$ for the simple Weyl representatives. Define the morphism $F_+:U_1^+\to U_0^+$ in the ordered product coordinates by keeping every parameter $z_\gamma$ and relabelling its root as $b(\gamma)$. This is a homomorphism: to multiply two ordered words, interchange adjacent factors by the displayed interchange laws and combine equal-root factors by addition. An interchange creates only roots of strictly greater height; descending induction on the finite height filtration therefore collects each word in finitely many steps. The same collection on both sides uses identical integers $C$ and identical parameter monomials, so the resulting coordinates agree over every $A$-algebra. For rank one this is just addition on its single factor, and for rank zero it is the map of trivial groups.

source.place: Lemma 6.2.8 and proof of Isogeny Theorem, Steps 2--4, pp.205--209; Proposition 5.1.16

proof.text:
In the extension criterion [lem-sfb-pinned-root-hom-extension-criterion] take $H=G_0$, $f_\alpha=x_{0,b(\alpha)}$, $h_\alpha=n_{0,b(\alpha)}$, and the preceding $F_+$. Torus equivariance and the reflection condition follow from step 1 and the torus-equivariant root maps in [lem-sfb-low-rank-universal-root-coordinates]. Its rank-one identities give $h_\alpha^2=b(\alpha)^\vee(-1)=f_T(\alpha^\vee(-1))$ and $(h_\alpha f_\alpha(1))^3=1$. In rank two the Weyl-word formula gives
$$(h_\alpha h_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}=\prod_{\gamma\in\Phi_1^+}b(\gamma)^\vee(-1)=f_T\left(\prod_{\gamma\in\Phi_1^+}\gamma^\vee(-1)\right)=f_T(t_{\alpha\beta}).$$
Finally the conjugation condition on $x_{1,\gamma}(z)$, $\gamma\ne\alpha$, has both sides equal to $x_{0,b(s_\alpha\gamma)}(u_{\alpha,\gamma}z)$, because the signs are universal. All hypotheses of the criterion are now checked; it produces $g$. Differentiating $g\circ x_{1,\alpha}=x_{0,b(\alpha)}$ gives the required pinning normalization. No coefficient was divided out.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, p.201; Example 6.2.6, pp.203--204; Lemma 6.2.8 and Step 4, pp.207--209

proof.text: We must establish uniqueness among all normalized homomorphisms, not just among maps preserving the chosen Weyl representatives. Let $f:G_1\to G_0$ be any homomorphism with the prescribed torus restriction. Apply [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] after each algebraically closed base-field specialization, with all $q_\alpha=1$. It gives a surjection with finite kernel, and its kernel coordinates have trivial additive factors, hence the kernel lies in the torus. Every root character is trivial on this torus kernel since $\alpha=h(b(\alpha))$. The centre formula [lem-sfb-adjoint-torus-root-coordinates] then makes the geometric kernel central. Consequently [lem-sfb-fibral-central-isogeny-recognition] makes $f$ finite and surjective over $A$, so in particular quasi-finite. The same applies to $g$. The last assertion of [lem-sfb-quasifinite-root-map-rigidity] now applies to any normalized $f$ and $g$: their torus restrictions and every simple-root tangent generator agree. It gives $f=g$ over the possibly nonreduced ring $A$.

source.place: Example 6.1.9, pp.191--192; Proposition 3.3.10; Proposition 6.1.13(2) and Corollary 6.1.15, pp.193--195

proof.text: For $J\subseteq\Delta_1$, [lem-sfb-small-centralizer-hom-amalgamation] supplies precisely the pinned split centralizers and inherited root data asserted in the statement. Step 1 identifies their root sets and bases, since $h_{\mathbf Q}$ identifies the indicated rational spans. Their torus lattice map is still $h$, with the same finite cokernel and coroot identities. Apply steps 1--3 to these restricted data to construct $g_J:G_{1,J}\to G_{0,b(J)}$. For $J=\Delta_1$ this is $g$. Otherwise, since $|\Delta_1|\leq2$, $J$ has size at most one. The simple positive and negative root maps and the Weyl representatives are inherited unchanged by [lem-sfb-low-rank-universal-root-coordinates]. Thus the two maps $g|_{G_{1,J}}$ and $G_{1,J}\xrightarrow{g_J}G_{0,b(J)}\hookrightarrow G_0$ agree on the full torus, its simple-root homomorphisms, and its simple Weyl representatives. The uniqueness clause of [lem-sfb-pinned-root-hom-extension-criterion], applied with source $G_{1,J}$ and target $G_0$, identifies them as scheme morphisms. This proves scheme-theoretic factorization, not just an assertion on geometric points. Step 4 for the restricted data identifies $g_J$ with their unique normalized homomorphism. When $J$ is empty the source is $T_1$ and the factorization is just $D_A(h)$.
